title: {{NAME}} and the Signal That Only the Smallest Could Hear
moral: True partnership means sharing the credit as generously as you share the work.

pages.content:
The Beacon Tower of Meridian City had stood for three hundred years, transmitting the navigational signal that every ship and aircraft in the region relied on. It had never failed. It had never even flickered. Which was precisely why, when it went silent at midnight on a Thursday, everyone whose instruments depended on it found themselves simultaneously lost in a way that had no obvious explanation and no obvious fix.

{{NAME}} arrived at the tower's base at dawn, the crimson suit still warm from the overnight flight across the city, to find GUIDE-1 already there. GUIDE-1 was the city's navigation robot: a tall angular machine of brushed silver, all sharp lines and rotating sensor fins, built specifically to interface with the tower's ancient signalling architecture. He had been here since the failure and his sensor panel expressed something that, in a human face, would have been an extended frustrated frown.

'I can reach eighty percent of the system,' GUIDE-1 reported without preamble. 'The remaining twenty percent is inaccessible. The transmission core is located inside the tower's original foundation chamber, built before any current access protocols. The passage is eleven centimetres wide.' His sensor fins rotated once. 'I cannot fit. You cannot fit. No standard-specification agent can fit.'

{{NAME}} looked at the eleven-centimetre gap in the tower's base with the evaluative focus of someone mentally running through every available option. It was a very small gap. It was also the only gap.

pages.content:
The fairy's name was Rue, and she appeared from inside the tower wall with the unhurried air of someone who had been listening to the whole conversation through a gap in the stone.

She was not, she made immediately clear, in the business of working for people. She was in the business of working with people, a distinction she delivered with the pleasant firmness of someone who has made it before and found it necessary to keep making it. Her wings were the blue-black of a mussel shell, shimmering in the earliest light, and her eyes were the particular amber of a fire that has found good fuel.

'I know the transmission core,' she said. 'Fairies have maintained this building since before it was built, in a manner of speaking. My family has been in these walls for twelve generations.' She looked at {{NAME}} and GUIDE-1 with equal, measured assessment. 'What I need is the repair protocol. The technical sequence. I can feel what's wrong, but I need to know what right looks like.'

GUIDE-1's sensor fins lifted fractionally. 'I can transmit the full repair sequence to a portable receiver,' he said. 'But the receiver would need to be brought inside the core for real-time guidance.' He paused. 'A receiver small enough for the passage would need to be—' 'Fairy-scale,' said Rue, already extending one precise hand. 'I assumed. I came prepared.' She was holding a component no bigger than a grain of rice. It was, {{NAME}} realised, already the correct part.

pages.content:
The repair took forty-seven minutes and required GUIDE-1 to transmit a continuous stream of technical data to the grain-of-rice receiver, which Rue wore behind her ear and which she apparently received as both sound and feeling simultaneously, a synesthetic experience she described briefly as 'like music that also tells you what to do.'

{{NAME}} monitored the tower's external outputs and relayed real-time status reports to GUIDE-1, who adjusted the protocol sequence in response, a three-way loop of information that moved faster and more accurately than any two of them could have managed. {{NAME}}'s flying ability proved critical twice: once to clear a jammed external vent that was back-pressuring the system, and once to intercept a curious crow who had decided the sensor fins were a roosting opportunity at a critical transmission moment. The crow was relocated diplomatically.

Deep inside the foundation chamber, Rue moved through the original architecture of the tower with the precise knowledge of someone raised in a building from childhood: every pipe, every wire, every ancient junction given to her as inherent understanding. She found the fault where GUIDE-1 had predicted it, replaced the rice-grain component with the rice-grain solution, and made three additional adjustments that the original protocol hadn't accounted for because they were fourteen generations of accumulated wear that no algorithm had tracked but a family of fairies had lived alongside.

The tower hummed. A single, clean, ascending note. The signal returned.

pages.content:
The Meridian City Navigational Authority sent three officials to the tower at eight in the morning, by which time the signal had been restored for an hour and the shipping lanes were clear and the overnight flight paths were corrected and everything that had gone wrong was precisely right again.

The officials were very glad to see {{NAME}} and GUIDE-1 and prepared to write a thorough commendation. They did not know about Rue, who was sitting in a tower-wall crevice listening with the expression of someone who has no strong feelings about official recognition and strong feelings about whether the work was done well.

{{NAME}} stopped the first official's speech at the third sentence. 'The repair was completed by three of us,' said {{NAME}}, and gave all three names with equal weight. The officials wrote all three names, including Rue's, in the official log, which had never contained a fairy name before and fit one perfectly.

GUIDE-1's sensor panel moved through several configurations and settled on one that, if it had belonged to a face, would have been warmth. 'The protocol was mine,' he said. 'The knowledge was hers. The coordination was yours. Attribution belongs to the mechanism that produced the result, not to the component with the highest visibility.' It was the most generous and accurate thing anyone had said all morning. Rue emerged from the crevice and gave him a look of frank approval.

pages.content:
By midmorning the city had gone back to being its usual self, which is to say busy and loud and full of the particular energetic chaos of a large place that has all its navigation working properly. Ships came and went through the harbour below with the smooth confidence of vessels that know exactly where they are.

The three of them sat on the tower's broad parapet in the morning sun, which was warm enough to take the edge off the night's cold, not warm enough to ask anything of you. GUIDE-1 had powered down his active systems to their rest state, sensor fins folded, his great silver body catching the light like a well-maintained sail. Rue sat on the parapet's edge with her blue-black wings spread to absorb the warmth, her amber eyes half-closed.

'My family found the original fault eighty years ago,' Rue said eventually, into the comfortable silence. 'They noted it in the wall-records. No one came to ask. They couldn't fix it themselves. It waited.' She said it without bitterness. Just as information. {{NAME}} thought about what it would mean to watch something need fixing for eighty years because no one had thought to ask the right people.

The city hummed below, finding its signal, knowing where it was.

Let the city's hum carry you down toward sleep now, quiet one. Like a ship that's found its bearing, like a light that's come back on. And somewhere in the tower wall tonight, Rue's family is updating their records, and this time, the right people know to ask.
